a: Wherever this order arrived
p: The same words open the Jews' mourning and the Jews' feast in Esther. Here the Gentiles feast instead.
b: Esther uses this phrase twice. When Haman's law goes out, "in every place the king's word and law arrived, the Jews mourned deeply" (Esther 4:3). When the second letter goes out, "wherever the king's word and his law came" the Jews feast (Esther 8:17). 3 Maccabees puts both scenes in one verse pair: the Gentiles feast (4:1) and the Jews mourn (4:2). The reader who knows Esther is meant to expect the second half of the pattern, and chapter 6 delivers it, with a feast in the very place set for the killing (6:30–31). On the decrees in Greek Esther, see the note on 7:1.

a: the Gentiles
p: The Greek ethnē means "the nations"; here it means the non-Jewish people of Egypt's towns.
b: The Greek Bible uses ta ethnē, "the nations," for the peoples who are not Israel (Hebrew goyim). In this book the word mostly means the non-Jewish townspeople of Egypt, the neighbors who cheer the decree (4:1; 5:6, 13), so the Plain says "the Gentiles." Where a king or a prayer speaks of peoples in general, it says "nations" (6:5, 26; 7:4). The writer does not make all Gentiles villains: some enemies weep (4:4), and earlier the Greeks of Alexandria pitied the Jews and hid them (3:8–10).

a: hardened
p: A rare verb: the Jews' neighbors had let their hatred set hard long before.
b: The participle prokateskirōmenēs comes from skiroō, "to harden," used of a callus or of plaster setting. It is very rare. The picture is of a grudge that set hard over years and now breaks out into the open ("openly," meta parrēsias). The writer wants readers to see that the king's decree did not create the hatred; it gave old hatred permission. Swete's two codices spell the word differently (A -kateskeirōmenēs, V -skērōmenēs), but the meaning is the same.

a: what pitiful place at all
p: Codex Alexandrinus has "most pitiful place"; Brenton's English reads "place at all inhabited."
b: Swete prints oiktistos topos, "most pitiful place," and Codex Venetus has the same word. In a list of districts, cities and streets, "inhabited" (Greek oikētos, one letter-group away) would fit better, and Brenton's 1844 English has "what place at all inhabited." The Plain keeps the reading of the manuscripts, which still makes sense: every place, sad as it now was, was full of wailing. The verse is a rhetorical question, a style the writer loves.

a: the pity all people share
p: Even some enemies wept. The writer allows that ordinary human pity reached across the hatred.
b: The Greek ton koinon eleon, "the common pity," is the pity owed to any human being, and the next clause adds a Greek commonplace: no one knows how his own life will end. The writer, who elsewhere calls the Gentiles "hateful" and "lawless" (6:9), admits that some of the Jews' enemies were moved. Historians note that the book's picture of Gentiles is mixed: the mob cheers (4:1), the Greeks of the city help in secret (3:8–10), and the king himself turns (6:22). For readers in Alexandria, who lived among Greeks, this mattered: the danger came from the court and the mob, not from every neighbor.

a: with their heads uncovered
p: A married woman showed her uncovered hair in public only in shame. These brides were stripped of it.
b: The brides had just had their hair perfumed for the wedding. Now it is fouled with dust, a sign of mourning, and they are paraded with their heads bare, akalyptōs. In the Bible, too, uncovering or loosening a woman's hair in public marks shame or accusation (Numbers 5:18), and Paul assumes that a woman who prays "with her head uncovered dishonors her head" (1 Corinthians 11:5). The writer piles up such contrasts (laments for wedding songs, ropes for garlands, 4:8) to make the reader feel the cruelty of the deportation.

a: like women torn by the cubs of a foreign breed
p: The Greek compares the deporters to the young of wild beasts from another race.
b: The phrase skymnois alloethnesin is strange: skymnoi are the cubs of lions or other beasts, and alloethnēs means "of another nation." The writer seems to mean that the young women were treated as if mauled by the whelps of a foreign people, the brutal young men of the king's guard. The image looks ahead to the real beasts of chapter 5. Some English versions smooth it into "outlandish insults" (so Brenton), which is a guess at the sense, not a rendering of the words.

a: Hades
p: The Greek name for the world of the dead, which the Greek Bible uses for the Hebrew Sheol.
b: Hadēs was the Greek name for the realm of the dead and its god. Jewish translators used it for Sheol, the grave and the land of the dead in the Hebrew Scriptures. 3 Maccabees uses it four times: the young husbands see it at their feet (4:8), the king swears to send the Jews there (5:42), they stand at its gates (5:51), and in the end they have walked into it and come back (6:31). The phrase "the gates of Hades" (5:51) is the one Jesus uses in Matthew 16:18.

a: Some had their necks nailed to the benches of the ships
p: The Jews of the countryside were shipped down the Nile to Alexandria, chained in the dark.
b: "They were brought down" (katēchthēsan) is the ordinary word for going downriver: the Jews of the Egyptian countryside (chōra) were taken down the Nile to Alexandria by boat. The zygoi are the crossbeams or rowing benches of the boats. Shut under a deck of planks (4:10), they could not see where they were going. The details are meant to recall the treatment of captives and slaves, and they set up the king's later charge against his own Friends, that they had treated the Jews "like slaves, or rather like traitors" (7:5).

a: Schedia
p: Schedia was a toll station on the canal from the Nile to Alexandria, about 30 kilometers from the city.
b: Strabo, who saw Egypt about 25 BC, says Schedia lay "four schoeni" from Alexandria, where a canal from the Canopic branch of the Nile ran toward the city. River traffic stopped there: there was a station for the boats that carried officials, a toll was taken on goods going up or down the river, and a bridge of boats (Greek schedia, "raft") gave the place its name (Geography 17.1.16). A schoenus was an Egyptian measure of a few miles, so the prisoners were landed short of the city and marched to the hippodrome.

a: the hippodrome in front of the city
p: A racetrack outside the walls: a place for crowds, chosen to make a public example of the Jews.
b: A hippodrome was a long track for horse and chariot races, with banks of seats for crowds. Alexandria's lay outside the walls, "in front of the city," and the writer says it was chosen for two reasons: everyone going in or out of the city would see the prisoners, and the Jews would be kept outside the city wall (Greek peribolos, the circuit wall). The crowd that gathers there in 5:24 and 5:46 is the audience for the planned show. The elephant story in Josephus (see the note on 6:21) does not name a hippodrome.

a: registered name by name
p: The king's register turns a census into a death list. Luke uses the same Greek word for the census of Augustus.
b: The verb apographō, "to register," and its noun apographē (4:15, 17) were the ordinary words for listing people and property for tax. Chapter 2 announced the census (laographia, 2:28) as the step that would reduce the Jews' standing. Here the register becomes a list of those to be killed in one day. The same noun stands in Luke 2:2: "It was the first such registration, carried out while Quirinius governed Syria." Scholars who date 3 Maccabees after the Roman census of Egypt in 24 BC think the book's readers had just lived through a registration that threatened their standing (see the chapter page).

a: For forty days
p: The register runs forty days, the Bible's number for a full time of testing.
b: Forty days is a fixed span of trial in the Scriptures: the rain of the Flood, Moses on the mountain, the spies in Canaan, Elijah's journey to Horeb, Jesus in the desert. 3 Maccabees gives exact dates for it later: from the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epiphi (6:38), which does come to forty days if both ends are counted (six days of Pachon, thirty of Payni, four of Epiphi). The careful count makes the story feel like a record, while the number itself tells the reader that this is a time of testing.

a: He held drinking parties in front of all the idols
t: A king who praises mute gods
p: Like Belshazzar, Ptolemy feasts and praises his idols while God's people suffer.
b: The scene recalls Belshazzar's feast: "As they drank wine, they sang the praises of their gods, made of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone" (Daniel 5:4). The writer mocks the idols in the words of the Psalms and the prophets: they are "mute" and "cannot speak." Compare "A mouth they have, but they cannot speak" (Psalm 115:5) and Habakkuk's "worthless gods that cannot speak" (Habakkuk 2:18). The king's god of choice is Dionysus, god of wine (2:29), so every drinking party in the book is also worship.

a: even the papyrus and the reed pens they wrote with had already run out
p: The register fails because Egypt runs out of papyrus and pens. Is this a miracle, or a joke?
b: Egypt was the land of papyrus, the paper of the ancient world, and its bureaucracy was famous for paperwork. That the king's clerks should run out of it is either a quiet miracle or a deliberate joke. Read as providence, the verse shows God working through the ordinary, as the next verse says outright (4:21): no angel appears, but the machine of the state jams. Read as satire, it mocks the all-powerful Ptolemaic state, which could not even finish a list. The two readings can stand together: the writer laughs at the king while praising God.

a: providence
p: Pronoia, "forethought," was a Greek philosophers' word. The writer gives it to the God of Israel.
b: Pronoia means "forethought" or "care planned ahead." Greek thinkers, especially the Stoics, used it for the divine reason that orders the world. Jewish writers in Greek took it over for God's care of his people: Wisdom of Solomon prays, "your providence, Father, steers it" (Wisdom 14:3, of a ship at sea). 3 Maccabees uses it at the two turning points of the plot, the failed register (4:21) and the king's forgetting (5:30). It is the book's own name for what the Hebrew Bible shows without naming, as in Esther.

a: Hermon
p: The officer is otherwise unknown. Ptolemaic kings did keep war elephants, but not five hundred.
b: Hermon is called "the master of the elephants" (elephantarchēs, 5:4, 45). He appears nowhere else. The Ptolemies did keep a corps of war elephants, caught in Africa. At Raphia in 217 BC, the battle with which this book opens (1:1–7), Polybius counts seventy-three elephants with Ptolemy and one hundred two with Antiochus (Polybius 5.79). The five hundred of 5:2 is far beyond that, one sign among several that the writer tells a story larger than life.

a: a great deal of unmixed wine to drink
p: Ancient armies roused war elephants with wine. Here the drink is meant to make them kill.
b: Greeks normally drank wine mixed with water; "unmixed" wine (akratos) was strong drink. Frankincense was costly temple incense, and mixing it into the wine (5:45) is either meant to madden the beasts or a mocking touch, sacred incense poured out for a slaughter. 1 Maccabees tells how the Seleucid army "showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries, to rouse them for the battle" (1 Maccabees 6:34). Josephus tells of elephants made drunk to trample the Jews of Alexandria under a later king (see the note on 6:21).

a: their merciful God and Father
p: The book's prayers call God "Father" three times, a way of praying that grew in Greek-speaking Judaism.
b: The Hebrew Bible calls God Israel's father mostly in poetry and prophecy: "You, LORD, are our Father" (Isaiah 63:16). In the prayers of 3 Maccabees the address becomes direct: "Father" (6:4, 8), and here "their merciful God and Father." The king himself says that God fights for the Jews "as a father for his sons" (7:6). Wisdom of Solomon prays the same way (Wisdom 14:3). For readers of the New Testament this is the world in which Jesus taught his followers to pray "Our Father" (Matthew 6:9), though the gospels make the address far more central and personal.

a: a splendid appearance
p: The book's key word: the Jews ask God to show himself, and in 6:18 he does.
b: Epiphaneia means a showing or appearing, especially of a god who steps in to help. Hellenistic kings took the idea for themselves: Ptolemy V, the son of this book's king, was called Epiphanes, "the god made manifest." 3 Maccabees gives the word back to God. The Jews pray for an appearance (5:8, 51; 6:9, "show yourself"), and in 6:18 God "let his holy face be seen" and sent his angels. 2 Maccabees uses the same word for God's rescues (2 Maccabees 3:24; 14:15).

a: sent the king a portion of sleep
t: The king who could not stay awake
p: In Esther sleep runs away from the king, and the Jews are saved. Here sleep falls on the king, and they are saved.
b: The turning point of Esther comes when "that night sleep ran away from the king" (Esther 6:1); awake, he reads the records and learns what Mordecai did. 3 Maccabees reverses the device: God sends sleep, and the king sleeps through his own massacre. Both stories make a king's bedroom the place where God acts unseen. The writer also calls sleep a gift: "he gives the one he loves sleep" (Psalm 127:2). Here it is given to an enemy, for the sake of God's people.

a: the one who is quick to make peace
p: The Greek eukatallaktos: God is easily won back. Paul's word for reconciliation is from the same family.
b: Eukatallaktos means "easily reconciled." Jews writing in Greek used the verb katallassō for God making peace again with his people after anger: "May he hear your prayers and be reconciled with you" (2 Maccabees 1:5; compare 2 Maccabees 7:33; 8:29). Paul uses the same verb but turns the direction around: "Through Christ he reconciled us to himself" (2 Corinthians 5:18). In 3 Maccabees people ask God to make peace; in Paul it is God who acts first to make peace with people.

a: Phalaris
p: The tyrant of Acragas in Sicily who was said to roast his victims inside a bronze bull.
b: Phalaris ruled Acragas (Agrigento) in Sicily in the 500s BC. Greek writers made him the model of a cruel tyrant: he was said to have shut his victims in a hollow bronze bull and lit a fire under it, so that their screams sounded like the bull's bellowing. To call Ptolemy "worse than Phalaris" (5:20) and "a Phalaris in every way" (5:42) is the writer's way of saying he was the worst of tyrants by Greek standards, not only by Jewish ones.

a: cruel sport
p: The Greek empaigmos means mockery, the same family of words used for the jeering of martyrs and of Jesus.
b: Empaigmos is "mockery" or "sport made of someone," from paizō, "to play." It is cruelty as entertainment. The Greek Bible uses the word for the abuse of the faithful, and Hebrews remembers those who "went through jeering and lashes" (Hebrews 11:36, the same noun). The verb is used of the soldiers who mocked Jesus (Matthew 27:29). In 3 Maccabees the guests of the king spend the night planning such sport, as the Philistines once called for Samson "so he can make us laugh" (Judges 16:25).

a: Gripped by complete ignorance
p: Twice the king forgets his own orders. The writer calls it God's doing; it also makes the king ridiculous.
b: First God sends sleep (5:11–12); then he puts "a forgetting" into the king's mind (5:28), so that the king no longer knows his own plan and even praises the Jews' loyalty (5:31). As providence, this is the strongest claim in the book: God rules the inner life of a hostile king. As a story, the forgetting king is a comic figure, an all-powerful ruler who cannot remember what he ordered the night before, and his Kinsmen say so (5:40). Readers in Alexandria could laugh at the court without saying anything against the living king.

a: He had put into the king's mind a forgetting
t: Compared with the Bible: God turns a king's mind
p: Agrees with the Bible's teaching that a king's heart is in God's hand. The miracle of forgetting goes beyond it.
b: Agrees. "Like water in irrigation ditches, the king's heart lies in the LORD's hand; he steers it wherever he likes" (Proverbs 21:1). Ezra says the LORD "had turned the Assyrian king's heart toward them" (Ezra 6:22), and Daniel 4 shows God taking a king's mind away and giving it back. Goes beyond. No book of the 66 has God erasing a king's memory overnight, twice. The closest is the reverse case, God making Pharaoh's heart stubborn (Exodus 14:4) so that his downfall would show God's glory.

a: They have shown me and my ancestors full and firm loyalty, beyond all others
p: The forgetful king blurts out what the book insists on: the Jews were the crown's most loyal subjects.
b: The irony is that the king tells the truth only when God has made him forget his plan. The claim is the book's thesis: the Jews of Egypt had served the Ptolemies faithfully (3:3; 6:25–26; 7:7). The Letter of Aristeas, another Greek Jewish writing from Egypt, says that Ptolemy I took Jewish captives to Egypt, "armed thirty thousand picked men and settled them in garrisons in the country districts" (Letter of Aristeas 13; compare 36). Whatever the numbers, Jewish soldiers did serve the Ptolemies, and the book speaks for their descendants.

a: who were raised with me
p: The king spares Hermon because he was brought up with him, a bond Hellenistic courts honored with a title.
b: Swete's text has systrophia, "a being bound together," which may stand for the more common syntrophia, "being raised together." At Hellenistic courts the boys raised with a prince were called his syntrophoi, "foster-brothers," and kept the title for life. Acts uses it of Manaen, "who had been raised alongside Herod the tetrarch" (Acts 13:1, Greek syntrophos). Brenton's English has "familiar friendship." Either way the king spares Hermon for old affection, while ordering the death of a whole people.
orig: τὴν τῆς συστροφίας στοργὴν (tēn tēs systrophias storgēn)

a: the God who shows himself
p: Epiphanēs, the title kings took, is here a title of God.
b: The Greek ton epiphanē theon is "the manifest God," the God who appears. The Seleucid king Antiochus IV and the Ptolemy after this book's king took the title Epiphanes. 3 Maccabees answers that only Israel's God truly shows himself, and in the next chapter he does (6:18, 39). In the same breath the Jews call him "King of kings," a title the Bible gives to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:37) and to the Lamb (Revelation 19:16). The two titles together deny a pagan king's claims to both.

a: Three times now you have ordered them wiped out
p: The plan fails three times: by sleep, by forgetting, and finally by angels.
b: The Kinsmen count three orders: the first before the sleep (5:2), the second before the forgetting (5:20), the third now (5:38). Stories often work in threes, and so does this one: God first delays the king by his body (sleep), then by his mind (forgetting), and the third time by open intervention (6:18–21). The Kinsmen's complaint also shows the human cost of a ruler's whims: the city is filling with mobs that want plunder (5:41).

a: the one "we may not enter,"
p: The king remembers the temple in Jerusalem that shut him out, the event of chapter 1.
b: The oath slips into the king's own voice: the temple is abaton hēmin, "not to be entered by us." This looks back to chapters 1–2, where Ptolemy tried to go into the sanctuary and was struck down (1:10–2:24). Gentiles were barred from the inner courts of the temple, and the charge that a Jew had brought Greeks in could start a riot (Acts 21:28). The king's threat, to burn the temple and stop its sacrifices forever, is what Antiochus IV did in part (1 Maccabees 1:44–47) and what Rome did in AD 70.

a: Other women held newborn babies at their breasts
p: The writer slows the story to a family's last embrace before the beasts arrive.
b: Parents and children, mothers and daughters, and nursing mothers with babies at the breast are named one by one. The writer uses such scenes often to move the reader (4:5–8). It also prepares the turn: in the next verse they remember God's help in the past, lay the babies down and cry out together (5:50–51). The weakest members of the community are the ones Eleazar points to in his prayer (6:14).

a: at the gates of Hades
p: A biblical picture of death as a city with gates. The Jews stand right at them.
b: The Scriptures picture death as a city or prison with gates: Hezekiah says he "must walk into the gates of Sheol" (Isaiah 38:10), and the sick "reached the gates of death" (Psalm 107:18). Wisdom of Solomon says God brings people "down to the gates of Hades" and "back up" (Wisdom 16:13), which is what happens in this story (6:31). Jesus promises that "the gates of Hades will not be stronger than" his church (Matthew 16:18).

a: a man named Eleazar
p: An old man of the countryside leads the prayer. The name recalls Aaron's son and the old martyr of 2 Maccabees.
b: Eleazar was a priestly name: Aaron's son and successor was Eleazar (Numbers 20:28), and Phinehas was his son (Numbers 25:7). 2 Maccabees tells of another Eleazar, "one of the foremost scribes, a man getting on in years," who died rather than eat pork (2 Maccabees 6:18). In Codex Venetus this Eleazar is "well known among the priests of the country" (see the variant), which brings him closer to the priestly line. In 3 Maccabees the old man does not die: his prayer is answered at once.

a: He hushed the elders around him
t: Did he stop them or calm them?
p: The Greek can mean he made the elders stop crying out, or that he calmed them so they could pray.
b: Katasteilas means "having checked, calmed, quieted." With the following infinitive it can mean that he stopped the elders from calling on God, so that he could pray for them all (so Brenton, "caused the presbyters ... to cease to cry out"), or that he calmed them as they prayed. The Plain says "hushed," which allows both. Either way one voice now speaks for the whole people, as Simon the high priest did in Jerusalem (2:1–20).

a: you steer all creation with tender mercy
p: Diakybernaō is a ship's word: God steers the world like a pilot. Wisdom of Solomon uses it too.
b: The verb diakybernaō comes from kybernētēs, "ship's pilot." Greek writers pictured the god who orders the world as its helmsman. Jewish prayer in Greek took the picture over: "your providence, Father, steers it" (Wisdom 14:3, the same verb, with "Father" and "providence" together, as in this book). The "tender mercies" (oiktirmoi) are the Greek Bible's word for God's compassion. Eleazar begins with God's rule over all creation before he asks for help in one hippodrome.

a: King, great in might, Most High, God Almighty
t: A prayer built on past rescues
p: Eleazar's prayer lists five rescues: Pharaoh, Sennacherib, the three in the fire, Daniel, Jonah.
b: The prayer (6:2–15) follows a pattern found across Jewish prayer: name God's past rescues, then ask him to act the same way now. Simon's prayer did this with the giants, Sodom and Pharaoh (2:4–8). Eleazar's list comes in order of history: the sea (6:4), Sennacherib (6:5), the furnace (6:6), the lions (6:7), and Jonah (6:8). Later Jewish prayer for fast days kept the same form: "He Who answered Abraham on Mount Moriah" will answer us, and so on through the fathers at the sea, Joshua, Samuel, Elijah, and Jonah in the belly of the fish (Mishnah Ta'anit 2:4). Hebrews 11:33–34 lists the same kinds of rescue as deeds of faith.

a: your own holy portion
p: Israel is the share God keeps for himself, as the Song of Moses says.
b: The picture comes from the Song of Moses: "For the LORD's own share is his people; Jacob is the inheritance measured out for him" (Deuteronomy 32:9). Eleazar's point is sharp: God's own portion is "dying unjustly as foreigners in a foreign land." The phrase fits Jews who had lived in Egypt for generations and still saw themselves as resident aliens there (6:36; 7:19).

a: the ruler of this Egypt long ago
p: "This Egypt": the prayer sets the Ptolemy in the hippodrome beside the Pharaoh of the Exodus.
b: Eleazar prays in Egypt, about a king of Egypt. The Pharaoh of the Exodus had chariots "in great numbers" (Exodus 14:7) and a boasting tongue; the Ptolemy of the hippodrome has elephants and a proud army. God drowned the first "in the sea" (Exodus 14:28; Exodus 15:4), and the reader waits to see what he will do with the second. The story answers: this time God does not destroy the king but turns him (6:22). The Exodus is the book's master story, and the feast in 6:30–36 is a new deliverance in the same land.

a: Sennacherib, the cruel king of the Assyrians
p: The Assyrian who boasted against Jerusalem and lost his army in one night (2 Kings 19).
b: Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day and mocked Israel's God (2 Kings 18–19). Isaiah's answer to him asks, "Who is it you have insulted and reviled?" (2 Kings 19:22). Then "the angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria: one hundred eighty-five thousand" (2 Kings 19:35). Judas Maccabeus uses the same example in prayer before battle (2 Maccabees 15:22). Here it prepares the angels of 6:18: as an angel struck Assyria, angels will turn back the king's army.

a: You made the red-hot furnace wet with dew
t: Compared with the Bible: the dew in the furnace
p: The dew comes from the Greek Daniel, not the Hebrew and Aramaic Daniel.
b: Agrees. In Daniel 3 the three refuse to worship the king's image, the flame kills the men who throw them in (Daniel 3:22), and they come out with "the hair on their heads ... not scorched" (Daniel 3:27), which this verse echoes in "unharmed down to a hair." Goes beyond. The dew is not in the Aramaic text. It comes from the Greek Daniel's Prayer of Azariah, where the angel makes the middle of the furnace "like a whistling wind of dew" (Greek Daniel 3:50; see the variant at Daniel 3:23). So the writer knew Daniel in Greek, with the Additions to Daniel. Codex Venetus lacks the dew here (see the variant).

a: because of jealous slander
p: Daniel's enemies envied him and slandered him; God brought him out unhurt.
b: Daniel 6 tells how the overseers "kept looking for something to use against Daniel" (Daniel 6:4) and trapped him by a law against prayer. "My God sent his angel to shut the lions' mouths" (Daniel 6:22), and "no injury at all was found on him" (Daniel 6:23). The parallel fits the Jews of the hippodrome closely: slandered by courtiers (3:2; 7:3), thrown to beasts, and rescued by God's angels. Hebrews counts those who "shut lions' mouths" among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:33).

a: showed him unharmed to all his own people
t: Compared with the Bible: Jonah's return
p: Jonah 2 ends with the fish spitting Jonah onto dry land. The return to his own people goes beyond the text.
b: Agrees. Jonah was "inside the fish" three days (Jonah 1:17) until "it vomited Jonah onto the dry land" (Jonah 2:10). The Greek word for the creature, kētos, is the one in the Greek Jonah and in Matthew 12:40, "the belly of the sea monster." Goes beyond. The Bible never says Jonah was shown "to all his own people"; the prayer adds it, perhaps as a picture of what the Jews hoped for themselves: to be brought back alive to their homes (7:20). Jonah is also the one rescue in the list where the person saved had disobeyed God, which fits the confession in 6:10.

a: you who hate arrogance
p: Misybris, a rare word: God hates hybris, the proud violence of the strong.
b: Misybris joins miseō, "hate," and hybris, the Greek word for arrogant, violent pride, the sin of tragic tyrants. Eleazar names the king's sin in Greek terms: the Jews are being "abused" (hybrizomenois, the same root) and are dying by the "senseless arrogance" of lawless men (6:12). The "holy ones" he speaks of are the people of Israel as God's own, not a special class of saints.

a: destroy us yourself, Master, by whatever death you choose
t: Better God's hand than the enemy's
p: If we have sinned, Eleazar says, punish us yourself, but do not let the idol-worshipers boast.
b: The prayer does not claim the Jews are sinless. It allows that their life abroad may be tangled in "ungodly acts" and asks that God judge them himself, not hand them to their enemies. David made the same choice: "let us fall into the LORD's hand, for his compassion runs deep. Into a human hand, let me not fall" (2 Samuel 24:14). The reason follows in 6:11: if God lets his people die at Gentile hands, the Gentiles will credit their idols.

a: in this land far from home
p: Apoikia is the Greek word for a colony; Eleazar uses it for the Jews' life in Egypt.
b: An apoikia was a colony, a settlement planted far from the mother city. Greek cities were proud of their colonies; Eleazar uses the word with a sense of exile. Later the book uses paroikia, "living as resident aliens" (6:36; 7:19). Both words say that Egypt, where Jews had lived for centuries, was not finally home.

a: 'Not even their God rescued them.'
p: The prayer borrows the Psalms' fear that God's name will be mocked if his people die.
b: The Psalms ask God to act for the sake of his name: "Why should the nations say, 'Where is their God?'" (Psalm 79:10; compare Psalm 115:2; Joel 2:17). Eleazar puts the taunt in the mouths of "the empty-minded," who "bless their empty gods," a wordplay in the Greek (mataiophrones ... mataiois). The same taunt was thrown at Jesus on the cross: "He has put his trust in God, so God should get him free now" (Matthew 27:43).

a: 'Not even when they were in the land of their enemies did I overlook them,'
p: Eleazar quotes Leviticus 26:44 in its Greek form: God will not forsake Israel even in exile.
b: The quotation is close to the Greek of Leviticus 26:44, "even when they are in the land of their enemies, I did not overlook them" (ouch hypereidon autous). The Hebrew, as the site's Plain gives it, says: "even while they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject them, and I will not loathe them." The Greek translators chose a verb meaning "overlook, disregard," and Eleazar's prayer depends on it. The Jews of Egypt were "in the land of their enemies," and they claim the promise made for exiles.

a: let his holy face be seen
p: The words of the priestly blessing, "may the LORD make his face shine," come true in the hippodrome.
b: The Greek epiphanas to hagion autou prosōpon, "showing his holy face," uses the same verb as the Greek of the priestly blessing: "May the LORD make his face shine toward you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25, Greek epiphanai kyrios to prosōpon autou). The prayer for an "appearance" (5:8, 51; 6:9) is answered in the language of Israel's oldest blessing. The "gates of heaven" are opened, as the gates of Hades were about to close (5:51).

a: two glorious angels, terrible to look at, who could be seen by everyone except the Jews
t: Angels the Jews could not see
p: The two angels terrify the army but are hidden from the Jews. Why?
b: The detail is unusual. In 2 Kings 6:17 God opens the eyes of Elisha's servant so that he sees the fiery army; here the faithful do not see the angels at all. Readers have offered reasons. Faith, not sight: the Jews are saved without a vision, as they prayed without one. The angels are only God's hands: the writer may be careful not to give angels the honor of the rescue (Wikipedia's summary of scholarship mentions this reading). A story device: the enemy's terror is the point, as with Heliodorus in 2 Maccabees 3:24–26, where two young men flog the man who tried to rob the temple.

a: The beasts turned back on the armed forces following them
p: Josephus tells a similar story, set under Ptolemy VIII, with drunken elephants turning on the king's men.
b: In Against Apion 2.53–55 Josephus says that Ptolemy VIII Physcon, a king of the later 100s BC, at war with the Jewish general Onias, had the Jews of Alexandria, with wives and children, bound and exposed to elephants made drunk. The elephants turned on Physcon's friends instead, the king saw a terrifying vision, and his concubine (Ithaca or Irene) begged him to stop. Josephus adds that the Alexandrian Jews keep that day as a festival. Most historians think both writers drew on one tradition; whether its core belongs to Ptolemy IV or VIII, or to neither, is debated.

a: You are ruling as if you were king
p: As in Greek Esther, the king turns on his counselors and clears himself.
b: The king now says his Friends were "ruling as if [they] were king" (parabasileuete) and plotting against him. Greek Esther does the same in Addition E: the king's second letter blames Haman, a "Macedonian" foreigner who abused the king's kindness (see the variant at Esther 8:12). In both, a pagan king rewrites events so that his own decree becomes the work of evil advisers, and his letter of protection follows (7:1–9). The Bible's Esther gives the king no such speech.

a: your benefactor
p: Euergetēs, "benefactor," was a royal title. The king claims it while his decree tortures his subjects.
b: Greek cities honored their patrons as euergetai, and kings used the word as a title: this king's father was Ptolemy III Euergetes. The rebels in 3:19 are those who will not honor their "benefactors." Jesus says plainly what such titles hide: "those who use their power over them are given the title 'Benefactor'" (Luke 22:25).

a: They have faithfully held the strongholds of our country for us
p: The king remembers that Jews guarded his forts. The Letter of Aristeas says the same.
b: The king's words agree with other Jewish writing from Egypt. The Letter of Aristeas says the first Ptolemy settled Jewish soldiers "in garrisons in the country districts" (Letter of Aristeas 13), and its royal letter says the king's father "built fortresses and placed them in their charge" (Letter of Aristeas 36). The book's readers knew themselves as descendants of such soldiers. That is why the charge of disloyalty (3:7; 7:4) hurt, and why the king's reversal stresses their service.

a: the sons of the Almighty, heavenly, living God
p: A pagan king calls the Jews God's sons, as the king does in Greek Esther's Addition E.
b: Israel is God's son in the Exodus story: "Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22). Hosea promises that Israel will be called "Children of the living God" (Hosea 1:10), a verse Paul applies to Gentiles as well (Romans 9:26). Greek Esther has the Persian king confess that the Jews are "children of the Most High, the most mighty living God" (Addition E, see the variant at Esther 8:12). 3 Maccabees uses the same device: the persecutor himself names the persecuted as God's sons (also 7:6).

a: celebrate their rescue
p: The Greek sōtēria, "rescue, deliverance," was also the name of a thank-festival. The Jews keep one.
b: Sōtēria agagein is "to hold a deliverance feast." Greek cities kept such feasts, called Sōtēria, to give thanks for rescue from war or plague. The writer gives the Jews their own: a seven-day feast at the king's expense, held "in the very place" meant for their death. The same word family runs through the end of the book: "a cup of rescue" (6:31), "Savior of Israel" (6:32; 7:16), "a drinking feast for their rescue" (7:18). The Plain renders it "rescue" throughout; it is the ordinary Greek word for "salvation."

a: a cup of rescue
p: The Jews raise a cup of thanks, as the psalmist promised to do.
b: The Greek kōthōn was a soldier's drinking cup, and then a drinking party. "A cup of rescue" calls to mind the psalm of thanks after rescue from death: "I will raise the cup of rescue and call on the LORD's name" (Psalm 116:13; Greek Psalm 115:4, potērion sōtēriou). The psalm begins with the cords of death and the distresses of Sheol (Psalm 116:3), which fits people who were "near to Hades, or rather already walking in it."

a: the song of their ancestors
t: Claude's theory: the Song of the Sea
p: The "song of their ancestors" may be the Song of Moses at the sea, sung again in Egypt.
b: The writer does not say which song. Claude's suggestion: the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) fits best. Eleazar's prayer opened with Pharaoh drowned in the sea (6:4), the story is set in Egypt, and the God praised here is "maker of wonders," the phrase of Exodus 15:11 (Greek poiōn terata; here teratopoion). The Song is also followed by dancing (Exodus 15:20), as here. This is a guess built on these links; "the song of their fathers" could also mean the Psalms in general, or the Hallel Psalms.

a: for their whole community of resident aliens
p: Paroikia is life as a resident alien. The Jews of Egypt still thought of themselves that way.
b: A paroikos was a foreigner living in a city without full rights. The Greek Bible uses the word for Abraham in Canaan and for Israel in Egypt (Acts 13:17, "while they were living as foreigners in the land of Egypt"). 3 Maccabees uses it of Egypt's Jews in its own day (also 7:19). 1 Peter takes over the word for Christians: "live in fear during your time as resident aliens" (1 Peter 1:17), almost the same Greek phrase as 7:19.
orig: ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν παροικίαν αὐτῶν (epi pasan tēn paroikian autōn)

a: they set the days we have mentioned to be kept as days of joy
p: The rescued Jews found a yearly festival, as the Jews of Esther did Purim.
b: The parallels with Esther are close. There the Jews turned the days of rescue into "a day of feasting and joy" (Esther 9:17) and made it binding "for their children after them" (Esther 9:27–28). Here they set "a rule ... for all generations" (6:36), and later found a second feast at Ptolemais (7:19). Esther's feasting comes after the thirteenth of Adar, on the fourteenth (Esther 9:17); here the feasting lasts "until the fourteenth" (6:40). The writer adds a Jewish warning Esther does not give: the days are "not for the sake of drinking and gluttony."

a: from the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epiphi
p: Pachon and Epiphi are Egyptian months; the forty days and the three days are counted exactly.
b: The writer dates by the Egyptian calendar, not the Jewish one. Pachon was the ninth month and Epiphi (Coptic Epip) the eleventh, with Payni between them. Counting both ends, the twenty-fifth of Pachon to the fourth of Epiphi is forty days, as 4:15 said. In the Coptic calendar, which still uses these names, Epip begins on 25 June of the Julian calendar, so the fifth to the seventh of Epiphi fall on 29 June to 1 July. Whether the ancient Egyptian calendar matched those days in Ptolemy IV's reign is a separate question.

a: King Ptolemy Philopator to the governors in Egypt
p: The second royal letter undoes the first (3:12–29), like Greek Esther's Additions B and E.
b: The book gives two royal letters, the decree of death (3:12–29) and this letter of protection (7:1–9). Greek Esther does the same with Addition B, the first letter against the Jews (see the variant at Esther 3:13), and Addition E, the second letter that blames Haman and calls the Jews God's children (see the variant at Esther 8:12). The Hebrew Esther only reports its letters (Esther 3:12–15; 8:9–14). Which book borrowed from which is debated. The letter opens and closes in the form of real Greek letters: "greetings and good health" and "Farewell" (compare Acts 15:23; Acts 23:26).
r: 3:12–29; Esther 3:13; Esther 8:12; Esther 3:12–15; Esther 8:9–14; Acts 15:23; Acts 23:26

a: the great God
p: A pagan king writes of "the great God" guiding him. The phrase can be heard two ways.
b: In the first letter the king thanked "the gods" for his victory (3:14). Now he credits "the great God." A Greek reader might hear a polite reference to whatever god the king honored; a Jewish reader would hear the God of Israel, whom the letter goes on to call "the God of heaven" and "the Most High God" (7:6, 9). The writer leaves the first line open and makes the rest of the letter plain, so that the king's change of mind is also a change of God.

a: the ill will these people have toward the other nations
p: The charge that the Jews hate other peoples, in Haman's words and in Greek writers, now in the king's mouth.
b: Haman told the king that the Jews' "laws are unlike any other people's" (Esther 3:8), and Addition B calls them a people hostile to all others. The same charges were made in chapter 3 of this book (3:7, 19, 24). Now the king quotes them only to reject them as the slander of malicious Friends. The book's answer is the one the Greek Esther also gives: the Jews keep apart in food and worship (3:4), but they are loyal subjects.

a: the custom of the Scythians
p: The horsemen north of the Black Sea were the Greeks' favorite example of savages.
b: The Scythians were nomad horsemen of the steppes north of the Black Sea. To Greeks they stood for wildness and cruelty, as in 2 Maccabees 4:47, where innocent men are condemned who "would have walked away blameless even if they had spoken before Scythians." Paul names them in a list of the most foreign peoples: "barbarian, Scythian, slave or free" (Colossians 3:11). The king says his Friends were worse than the Scythians.

a: as a father for his sons
p: A pagan king confesses that the God of heaven fights for the Jews as a father for his sons.
b: Moses reminds Israel that "the LORD your God carried you, the way a man carries his son" (Deuteronomy 1:31). The book's own prayers call God "Father" (5:7; 6:4, 8), and the king echoes them. On God as father in this book see the note on 5:7.

a: not a human being, but the Most High God
p: The king warns his officials that harm to the Jews would make God their enemy.
b: The king's warning is that opposing these people is opposing God. Gamaliel said the same of the apostles: "You might even turn out to be fighting against God" (Acts 5:39). In Esther, Haman's own wife foresees his fall before Mordecai (Esther 6:13). Here the warning is written into law for every governor in Egypt.

a: who had willfully broken faith with the holy God and God's law
p: Jews who had given up the Law, probably by joining the cult of Dionysus to gain citizenship (2:30–33).
b: The "renegades" are Jews who had taken the king's offer in 2:30: initiation into the mysteries of Dionysus in exchange for equal citizenship. Some "gave themselves up readily and lightly" (2:31), and the faithful already "judged them enemies of the nation" and shut them out (2:33). Now the faithful ask for leave to punish them. The writer speaks of them only as transgressors "for the sake of their stomachs" (7:11): people who had eaten what the Law forbids. On how to read what follows, see the chapter page.

a: for the sake of their stomachs
p: The Greek "for the belly's sake" means eating forbidden food: the renegades broke the food laws.
b: Gastros heneken, "for the sake of the belly," is a sharp phrase. It sums up apostasy as a matter of food: those who had joined the king's feasts and sacrifices had eaten what the Law forbids (compare 3:4, where Jews keep apart "in the matter of food"). In 1 Maccabees the faithful "accepted death rather than be made unclean by food" (1 Maccabees 1:63). Paul uses the same picture for false teachers: "Their god is the belly" (Philippians 3:19; compare Romans 16:18).

a: without needing any royal authority or review
t: Compared with the Bible: killing apostates
p: The Law punished those who led Israel to other gods, after a careful inquiry. Here there is no trial at all.
b: Agrees, in part. Deuteronomy commands death for anyone who entices Israel to "serve other gods" (Deuteronomy 13:6–10), and the zeal of the Levites (Exodus 32:26–28) and of Phinehas (Numbers 25:7–8) is praised; 1 Maccabees hails Mattathias for killing an apostate at the altar (1 Maccabees 2:24–26). Conflicts. The Law requires a city to "look into it, search it out, and ask questions with care" first (Deuteronomy 13:14); here the king grants killing "without any ... review." And the New Testament forbids it: Jesus rebukes the disciples who want fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54–55), and Paul says, "never take revenge yourselves" (Romans 12:19).
r: Deuteronomy 13:6–10; Deuteronomy 13:14; Exodus 32:26–28; Numbers 25:7–8; 1 Maccabees 2:24–26; Luke 9:54–55; Romans 12:19

a: shouting "Hallelujah!"
p: The Greek writer keeps the Hebrew shout: "Praise the LORD!"
b: The Greek has to allēlouia, the Hebrew hallelu-yah, "praise Yah," written in Greek letters. It was a shout from the Psalms that Greek-speaking Jews kept in Hebrew, as Christians still do. Tobit 13:18 has it in the songs of the new Jerusalem, and Revelation 19:1 in the songs of heaven. Here it is shouted by priests and people as they leave the king with leave to kill.

a: who had been defiled
p: The renegades had made themselves unclean by pagan worship and forbidden food.
b: Memiamménōn, "defiled," is the word for ritual uncleanness: eating unclean food, taking part in idol worship, or being branded with the ivy leaf of Dionysus (2:29). The writer calls the renegades "of their own people" (homoethnē): the killers and the killed are Jews. Codex Venetus says only that they "punished" them (see the variant).

a: more than three hundred men
p: In Esther the Jews of Susa kill three hundred of their enemies. Here the three hundred are fellow Jews.
b: "In Susa they killed three hundred men" (Esther 9:15). The number here is likely chosen to echo it. But there is a large difference: in Esther the dead are "those who hated them," armed enemies (Esther 9:1, 16); in 3 Maccabees they are Jews who gave up the Law, killed after the danger had passed, and the day of killing is turned into "a day of joy and gladness." Many modern readers find this the hardest passage in the book (see the chapter page).

a: who had held fast to God even to death
p: The faithful are those who would have died rather than give up God, as the risen Christ asks of his churches.
b: The Greek is "those who had held God until death." They did not have to die, but they were ready to. The words recall the call in Revelation: "Stay faithful all the way to death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10), and here, too, the faithful leave "crowned" with flowers. In early Christian writing such readiness becomes the mark of the martyrs.

a: Ptolemais, which is called "Rose-Bearing"
p: Several towns in Egypt bore the name Ptolemais; this one was known for its roses.
b: Ptolemaic kings founded or renamed many towns after themselves, so "Ptolemais" alone does not tell us where the Jews stopped. The writer marks this one by its nickname, rhodophoros, "rose-bearing," and says the fleet waited there seven days. It was on the river route home, since the Jews go back "on land and sea and river" (7:20).

a: for all their time as resident aliens
p: The same Greek phrase stands in 1 Peter 1:17 for Christians living in the world.
b: The Greek ton tēs paroikias autōn chronon, "the time of their sojourning," is the phrase of 1 Peter 1:17, "live in fear during your time as resident aliens" (ton tēs paroikias hymōn chronon). 1 Peter was written to Christians scattered across Asia Minor (1 Peter 1:1) who faced slander from their neighbors. The words that the Jews of Egypt used for their life in a foreign land became the church's words for its life in the world. On the word see 6:36.

a: to keep these days as days of joy
p: The only outside evidence is Josephus: the Jews of Alexandria kept a festival for a rescue from elephants.
b: The book says the days were fixed by the community in Alexandria (6:36) and again at Ptolemais (7:19), and written on a pillar (7:20). No calendar of Jewish festivals names it. Josephus, writing about AD 95, says that after the elephants turned on Ptolemy VIII's men "the Alexandrian Jews do with good reason celebrate this day" (Against Apion 2.55, Whiston's translation). If that is the same festival, it was kept in the first century AD, though the two writers tie it to different kings. Some scholars think the book was written to explain such a festival.

a: a place of prayer
p: In Egypt Jewish meeting houses were called proseuchē, "prayer." Acts uses the word at Philippi.
b: The Greek proseuchē means "prayer," and in Egypt it was the usual name for a Jewish meeting house. Dedication inscriptions show that such houses of prayer existed by the 200s BC. So the Jews mark the place of rescue as Jews of Egypt marked their communities: with a house for prayer and reading the Law. Luke uses the same word at Philippi: "We expected to find a place of prayer there" (Acts 16:13).

a: shook them down
p: Diaseiō, "shake down," is the word John the Baptist used to the soldiers.
b: The verb diaseiō literally means "to shake thoroughly," and in everyday Greek it meant to extort money by threats. John the Baptist tells soldiers, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force" (Luke 3:14, the same verb). The Jews come home to a land where no one dares to shake them down for their goods; the next verse says the goods taken from them are returned.

a: Blessed be the Rescuer of Israel
p: The book ends with a blessing on God as Israel's rescuer, a title Paul quotes from Isaiah.
b: Rhystēs, "rescuer," comes from the verb rhyomai, "to rescue," that runs through the prayers (5:8; 6:6, 10-11). Isaiah 59:20 in Greek says "the one who rescues will come for Zion's sake" (ho rhyomenos), and Paul quotes it: "The Deliverer will come out of Zion" (Romans 11:26). The closing "Blessed be ... Amen" is the form that ends the books of the Psalms (Psalm 41:13; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52).
